summary: Brick-and-stucco light of 1903 on Fort Casey's bluff at Admiralty Inlet, the second light here since 1861. Discontinued in 1922; now a state-park museum open in season.

lens.where: Lost after the 1927 lantern removal; the museum shows a fourth-order lens from Alki Point and a 2003 Coast Guard loan, both not the original

structures.type: conical tower with attached two-story residence
structures.note: Built by the Army Corps of Engineers (LighthouseFriends: the War Department, under Major John Millis); designed by Carl W. Leick

structures.type: square wooden tower on the keeper's house
structures.note: Relocated for Fort Casey in 1899-1901; dismantled by the Army in 1928

access.note: Open in season within Fort Casey State Park; LighthouseFriends gives noon to 4 p.m. daily in June, July and August.

facts.agency: Washington State Parks (Fort Casey State Park)

events.note: Ten acres bought on Red Bluff from Dr. John Kellogg for $400
Two-story keeper's house with a square wooden tower on its roof, completed January 1861
First exhibited January 21, 1861 (the archive gives 1860 as the year established)
123 more acres bought from Dr. Kellogg for $7,200 for Fort Casey
Station moved for the fortification works; the Board's 1899 report says it had to be moved
Old reservation exchanged for two pieces of ground nearby
New brick-and-stucco tower and residence built for the Army
Activated June 25, 1903
Fourth-order lens moved from the old tower into the new lantern
Changed from white to red on May 1, 1919, for reasons the sources do not give
Last night June 30, 1922 per the keeper's log; decommissioned July 1, 1922
Iron-and-glass lantern removed and placed on the New Dungeness tower
Original fourth-order lens removed and went missing
Army dismantled the old wooden lighthouse; lumber used for a house on south Whidbey Island
Coast Guard merged with the Lighthouse Service
Transferred to the War Department in March 1941; used as K-9 Corps barracks
Washington State Parks acquired 100 acres of the fort's battery area
Island County Historical Society and State Parks began restoration, including a rebuilt iron-and-glass lantern room
Fort Casey State Park, including the lighthouse, added to the Central Whidbey Island Historic District listing (district listed December 12, 1973)
Included in the Postal Service's five-stamp lighthouse set
Coast Guard lent the museum a fourth-order lens identical to, and possibly, the one that went missing
Replica lantern room placed on the tower on August 23, 2012
Major restoration begun after the legislature approved $1.7 million

corrections.why: The light was first exhibited on January 21, 1861 (HistoryLink; LighthouseFriends). The archive's 1860 is the year the station was established, and the record's first_lit should carry the lighting date.

The archive gives the light at 127 feet above mean high water, and HistoryLink gives 127 feet above sea level (38.7 m). The 40 m (130 ft) figure in the record matches Wikipedia, which we use only for leads.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends prints Nessel's log entry under December 15, 1897, but its own text places the Point Wilson light nineteen years after the 1861 start. HistoryLink dates the commissioning to December 15, 1879. The story follows 1879.

The last keeper's log reads 'after tonight' on June 30, 1922; HistoryLink gives July 1, 1922 as the decommissioning date. The story uses both: the last night was June 30, and the station was decommissioned July 1.
The archive and LighthouseFriends spell Lawrence; HistoryLink spells Laurence. The record uses the archive's spelling in the keeper roster and notes the variant.

The Board's 1899 and 1901 reports and HistoryLink describe a move of the old house, and HistoryLink and LighthouseFriends date its dismantling to 1928. Wikipedia gives an 1890 relocation and is not used.

notes_for_editor: No storms, wrecks or rescues were found for this station in the sources read, so the story has no chapter for them. The archive's Admiralty Head place description, seen only in search results and not fetched, says the Army demolished the old light during the Spanish-American War; the Board's 1899-1901 reports and HistoryLink show a move, and the old house was dismantled in 1928. That description is not used. Wikipedia's 1890 relocation date is leads only. The Seattle Post-Intelligencer obituary is quoted through HistoryLink; a Chronicling America search for it (Washington, 1897) did not turn up the page, so it is cited as HistoryLink quotes it. LighthouseFriends' Flora Pearson material, including the 1875 inspector's order, is her memoir as LighthouseFriends prints it. Hans P. Score's log is quoted through LighthouseFriends. The 1900 table (scan page 43) is an appropriations table read by OCR; the figure is $12,000 and the line reads 'removal and reconstruction of buildings, additional'. The fourth-order lens currently on display came from Alki Point and was lent in 2003 by the Coast Guard; neither is the original. LighthouseFriends' hours are undated; HistoryLink, written in 2021, says the lighthouse is open seasonally. The keeper Georgianna Pearson's married name is given by HistoryLink as Terry; the archive keeps the maiden name. No living person is named.
